name: Industrious Labs (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result's parts at the defaults, harms and goods alike. The rule's compliance costs (most of the size) and the Los Angeles basin's cleaner air fall in the United States; the tonnes' heat deaths are spread by world population.
summary: Industrious Labs (Cincinnati) campaigns to cut emissions from US heavy industry: steel, aluminium, cement, industrial heat and landfills. This model counts the one rule it helped win in 2023-2024, South Coast AQMD's Rule 1146.2 (2024), which moves about a million water heaters, boilers and pool heaters in the Los Angeles basin to heat pumps as they wear out, against its spending in those years (about $3.7 million a year, from Tides Foundation's grants to it; its own accounts aren't public), with its steel, aluminium and other work as a share of that value. At the defaults the rule's compliance costs (the district's own figure, about $60 a tonne) outweigh what its tonnes and cleaner air are worth on the site's scale, so the result is a small net harm, about -0.003 years of healthy life per $1,000; it turns positive if the basin’s street-level smoke kills about six times more per tonne than our middle figure, the biggest uncertainty. The branch is discounted for missing data: no tonne is measured for its work.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The tonnes a year the period's won rule would avert once in effect.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Air pollution these tonnes carry
sections.explainer: Every tonne avoids its heat deaths; a tonne from burning less fossil fuel near people also avoids air-pollution deaths. These rows say how much of the shared air-pollution rate applies to this charity's tonnes (docs/normalization.md 2.5); the rates themselves stay shared.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in tonnes
sections.explainer: The won rule's compliance costs (units of value) enter the tonnes only through the site's fixed bridge (docs/normalization.md 2.6).

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Share of Industrious Labs' spending paid through Tides Foundation
rows.explainer: Some funders may give to the company directly, as in 2022, when Tides paid nothing and the budget was $3 million with 12 staff (Axios, 25 October 2022). Tides' $2.3 million in 2023 is below that launch budget while the group grew into five sectors, so Tides is unlikely to be the whole budget. Our judgment, 75% (45% to 100%); the spending below is Tides' grants over this share.

rows.label: Years in the period
Average yearly spending 2023-2024, in 2024 prices, ÷ 2024's

rows.label: Cost of a typical year of 2023-2024, in 2024 dollars
South Coast AQMD Rule 1146.2: tonnes of CO₂ a year averted once fully in effect
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate, 2.2 million tonnes, 1.6 to 2.5): gas no longer burned by about 1.07 million pool heaters, large and tankless water heaters, small boilers and process heaters in the Los Angeles basin, less the power their heat pumps draw, from the district's own per-unit energy figures.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e a year the rule would avert once in effect, upstream methane included
rows.explainer: Gas not burned is also gas not leaked upstream: the combustion CO₂ grossed up by the methane share of the cut (conversion section, row methane_share).

rows.label: Share of the win due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%): the part of a won rule that is the advocates' doing rather than what the district, the state's climate laws and the federal ozone deadline would have brought at the same time. The rule is in, so this is not a chance of winning; Industrious Labs' part of the advocates' work is the attribution row.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Years from the rule (2024) until its tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The rule's own dates in place of the shared wait for regulations: units switch when they wear out, from 2026 in new buildings and 2029-2033 in existing ones, over lives of 15 to 25 years, so the middle of the cut is about 2040 (facts: climate, 16 years, 10 to 20).

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the unit's conversion then discounts the heat deaths from the year the tonne is avoided, so nothing is discounted twice.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
Expected tonnes a year of the period, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The period's one modelled win: its tonnes a year × the advocacy share × its discounted years, spread over the period's two years.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: how far the tonnes from the district's figures should be trusted
rows.explainer: The tonnes are our arithmetic on the district's ex-ante per-unit gas and electricity use (pool heaters run less than assumed in some homes, more in others; the mix of the 60,000 commercial units is inferred), not measured cuts. Our judgment, 0.8 (0.5 to 1.1), as for Clean Air Task Force's regulator-estimated rules; delivery and delays are in the implementation row, not here.

rows.label: Share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this rule (facts: climate, 75%, 50% to 90%): building codes, rebates and the market would have moved some units to heat pumps in the years counted anyway.

rows.label: Industrious Labs' share of the advocates' resources behind the rule
rows.explainer: Industrious Labs calls Rules 1146.2 and 1153.1 'two landmark victories' it secured, organised the first rally for an industrial-boiler rule (Canary Media, 7 June 2024) and intervened to defend the rule in court with the People's Collective for Environmental Justice and the Sierra Club; Earthjustice was co-counsel and lead legal voice, and the Coalition for Clean Air, the Natural Resources Defense Council, RMI and many community groups pushed the district's 2022 plan that the rule carries out. Our judgment, 15% (5% to 35%) of all the groups' work.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of the rule's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this rule (facts: climate, 70%, 40% to 90%): upheld in district court (2025) and the Ninth Circuit (July 2026), but the 2027 technology review could delay the later dates.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no tonne is measured for Industrious Labs' work; the tonnes are our arithmetic on the regulator's figures and its part a judgment.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Other work of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Most of the spending went to steel, aluminium, cement and landfills, whose results so far are small or lost: DOE's 2024 clean-steel and aluminium awards were mostly withdrawn (SSAB pulled out, DOE dismantled the programme in May 2025, Cleveland-Cliffs moved its Middletown award to coal in August 2026), U.S. Steel relined its Gary blast furnace for 20 more years (2025); Century Aluminum's award led to a planned Oklahoma smelter with EGA whose power is not yet known. Still pending or small: Cleveland-Cliffs has put off relining a Burns Harbor blast furnace three times, EPA's 2024 coke-oven and steel air-toxics rules were restored after a 2025 exemption, the Colorado and California landfill-methane rules, the district's commercial-oven Rule 1153.1, the California industrial-heat laws AB 2083 (2024) and AB 1280 (2025), and the steel communities' training cohort. Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 30% of the modelled value (5% to 100%: a coal furnace not relined would be worth more than the rule).

rows.label: Side effect: refrigerant leaking from the new heat pumps, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Heat pumps hold refrigerants that warm the climate when they leak, which the tonnes above leave out. For US home heat pumps NREL's simulation puts leaks at about 0.07 tonnes a year against 2.5 to 4.4 tonnes cut (facts: climate.us_heat_pump_tco2e_per_household_year, its note), about 2%. Our judgment, −2% (−4% to 0).

rows.label: Rule 1146.2: units switched on average over 2026-2057, as a share of all

source.title: South Coast AQMD (May 2024), Draft Socioeconomic Impact Assessment for Proposed Amended Rule 1146.2
source.note: Each category's average yearly fuel saving (Table 3) over its per-unit saving (Table 2) gives the units switched in an average year: pool heaters 464,600 of 710,000, tankless water heaters 173,400 of 300,000, other units 38,500 of 60,000; 676,500 of 1,070,000 = 0.63. Range: the categories' own shares, 0.58 to 0.65, widened a little.

rows.explainer: The district's cost is an average over 2026-2057, while units are still being replaced; the tonnes are counted once every unit has switched. Dividing the cost by this share puts both on the same full-implementation footing.

rows.label: Rule 1146.2: compliance costs, units of value (negative)
rows.formula: -@compliance_costs.scaqmd_rule_1146_2_net_cost_per_year / scaqmd_phase_in_share * @cpi.usa_2024 / @cpi.usa_2023 * $uov_per_ln_consumption / (@public_funds.compliance_cost_payer_multiple * @united_states.ce_expenditure_per_person_2024) * p_success * discounted_years * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The won rule's compliance costs (docs/normalization.md 2.21): owners' extra cost for heat pumps and panel upgrades less their fuel savings (the district's analysis, $96.8 million a year on average over 2026-2057 at 4%), scaled to full implementation, in 2023 dollars moved to 2024's, valued as money lost by those who bear it, consumers and owners (@public_funds.compliance_cost_payer_multiple, 1.2 times average US consumption), on the log scale; over the same years and wait as the rule's tonnes, with the advocacy share, counterfactual, credit, delivered share and missing-data step, not the evidence adjustment (which is about the benefits).

rows.label: Compliance costs of the won rule, units of value per year of the period
rows.explainer: In the main chain (docs/normalization.md 2.21), spread over the period's two years. The unmodelled work's share isn't applied to costs: most of it won no rule.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes that are methane
rows.explainer: Gas a building stops burning also stops leaking upstream: the shared share for electrifying US buildings (facts: climate, 15%, 5% to 25%), weighted as the rule's one branch. The shared conversion values it by methane's own warming and ozone (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: Every CO₂ tonne is gas no longer burned in a water heater, boiler or pool heater at street level; the methane share carries no smoke (its ozone is counted through the methane share).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne cut, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this rule (facts: climate, 0.05, 0.01 to 0.4): street-level NOx in the country's worst ozone basin, more smoke per tonne than electrifying an average US home (0.02), the top the advocates' count of 2,800 early deaths avoided.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tco2e unit's conversion (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly (none here)
rows.explainer: 0: the rule's smoke is in air_pollution_weight, so nothing is counted twice.

rows.label: The won rule's compliance costs, in tonnes of CO₂e (negative)
rows.formula: compliance_uov_per_year / (($deaths_per_tco2e * $climate_heat_share * ((1 - methane_share) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -$climate_heat_death_delay + methane_share * @climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2 * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -@climate.methane_heat_death_delay) * (1 + @climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) * (@death_ages.heat_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.heat_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.heat_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.heat_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74) + ($deaths_per_tco2e * (1 - $climate_heat_share) * air_pollution_weight + extra_deaths_per_tco2e + methane_share * @climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane / (1 + ln(1 + $discount_rate) * @climate.methane_lifetime_years)) * (@death_ages.air_pollution_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74)) * $life_value_multiplier)
rows.explainer: Units of value into tonnes at what a tonne of these is worth on the site's scale (its heat and air-pollution deaths by age, as the conversion counts them), the bridge Clean Air Task Force's and Environmental Defense Fund's models use (docs/normalization.md 2.6).

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per year of the period
rows.explainer: The rule's expected tonnes × its adjustments, with the other work and the refrigerant side effect added as shares, less the rule's compliance costs in tonnes.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar
Staff pay as a share of programme cost
rows.explainer: The shared default for advocacy work (facts: staff_pay.share_advocacy); the company's accounts, which would give its own share, aren't public.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: The shared pay gap for advocacy staff (facts: staff_pay.gap_advocacy).

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: Industrious Labs' own figure (facts: next_dollar, docs/normalization.md 2.10): room 0.7 × use 0.6 × run 1.0 = 42% (20% to 75%). The model's dollar is its 2023-2024 spending over that period's wins. 1 in `published`: what the past average itself says.
